_note: Curated landmark witnesses for the timeline scatter. date_low/date_high = estimated copying date (AD). year_known = when it entered scholarship (discovery or publication). Dates are conventional ranges; the build session should confirm each against the INTF Liste (ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste) and Wikipedia's per-manuscript pages, and add ~15 more medieval minuscules to fill the lower-right of the plot.
sources: Bruce Metzger & Bart Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament, 4th ed. (2005)
Daniel Wallace, CSNTM manuscript counts (2013 tally: 128 papyri, 322 majuscules, 2926 minuscules, 2462 lectionaries = 5838)

witnesses.name: Rylands Papyrus
witnesses.note: Conventionally the earliest NT fragment; some date it later (2nd-3rd c.)

witnesses.name: P.Oxy. 2
witnesses.year_known_basis: Grenfell and Hunt found it at Oxyrhynchus on 13-14 Jan 1897; published in The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, vol. 1 (1898). Corrected from 1897 (find date) to 1898 (publication date, consistent with this dataset's convention of using publication/entry-into-scholarship year).

witnesses.name: Codex Vaticanus
witnesses.found: Vatican Library (catalogued 1475; usable photographic facsimile 1889-90; used by Westcott-Hort 1881)
witnesses.note: year_known here = first serious critical use; adjust if you prefer 1475 or 1889

witnesses.name: Codex Alexandrinus
witnesses.found: Gift to Charles I from Patriarch of Constantinople

witnesses.name: Codex Bezae
witnesses.found: Lyon; given to Cambridge by Beza

witnesses.name: Minuscule 2814 (formerly 1r)
witnesses.found: Erasmus's only Revelation manuscript; last verses back-translated from Latin

witnesses.name: Minuscule 1739
witnesses.year_known_basis: Corrected from 1879. Discovered/collated by Eduard von der Goltz at the Great Lavra, Mount Athos, and published in his 1899 monograph 'Eine textkritische Arbeit des zehnten Jahrhunderts' (Leipzig); this is what brought the manuscript's importance (copied from a 4th-century exemplar) into NT scholarship. Some secondary sources give 1897 for the visit; kept 1899 as the publication year per this dataset's convention.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 69 (Codex Leicester / Leicestrensis)
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 69': John Mill was permitted to use the manuscript at Oxford and collated it there in 1671 (as 'L'), for his 1707 Novum Testamentum; it had already been given to the Leicester Library by Thomas Hayne in 1641. Later re-collated by Tregelles (1852) and Scrivener (1855), and seen by Gregory (1883). Corrected from 1887 (J. Rendel Harris's later monograph on the codex, which was not the earliest scholarly use).
witnesses.found: Leicestershire Record Office (deposited by the City of Leicester), England

witnesses.name: Minuscule 81
witnesses.year_known_basis: Discovered/examined by Constantin von Tischendorf in 1853; dated by its own colophon to 1044. Formerly labelled 61a/61p by Gregory.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 104
witnesses.year_known_basis: Colophon-dated to 1087. Part of the Harleian collection (Robert Harley); catalogued in the British Museum's 1759 printed catalogue of the Harleian manuscripts (Harley MS 5537).
witnesses.verify_note: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 104' confirms it was purchased by John Covel, chaplain of the Levant Company at Constantinople, 1670-1676, and later examined by Mill, Griesbach, Bloomfield, Henri Omont (who described the British Museum's Harleian Greek manuscripts in 1884), and F.H.A. Scrivener -- but gives no single year for when it first entered scholarship, so this does not confirm or refute this dataset's 1759 (British Museum's printed Harleian catalogue) claim. Check the INTF Liste: https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste?docID=30104

witnesses.name: Minuscule 157
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 157': in 1788 the scholar Andreas Birch made a facsimile of the manuscript, calling it the most important New Testament manuscript except Codex Vaticanus; later examined by Johann Scholz, collated by Herman Hoskier, and seen by Gregory in 1886. (Refines this dataset's earlier 1780 estimate for the same Birch tour to the specific 1788 facsimile.)
witnesses.found: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. Urb. gr. 2, Rome

witnesses.name: Minuscule 205
witnesses.year_known_basis: Written by scribe John Rhosus for Cardinal Bessarion (with codices 354, 357); entered the Biblioteca Marciana via Bessarion's 1468 bequest and was first described in print in Anton Maria Zanetti's 1740 catalogue of the Marciana's Greek manuscripts.
witnesses.verify_note: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 205' confirms it was written for Cardinal Bessarion and sent to his library in 1468, and says it 'was added to the list of New Testament manuscripts by Griesbach' and 'examined by Birch and Burgon' and 'seen [by] C. R. Gregory ... in 1886' -- but gives no year for Griesbach's or Birch/Burgon's work, so this does not confirm or refute this dataset's 1740 (Zanetti's catalogue) claim. Check the INTF Liste: https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste?docID=30205

witnesses.name: Minuscule 209
witnesses.contents: Complete NT (Revelation quire added slightly later)
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 209': Hoskier reported that the printer/scholar Aldus used the manuscript to correct the Erasmian text in his Greek New Testament of 1518. It had earlier belonged to Cardinal Bessarion, present with him at the Council of Florence in 1439 (matching this dataset's 'found'); later examined by Birch, Engelbreth, Fleck, Rinck, and Burgon, and seen by Gregory in 1886. Corrected from 1788 (Birch's later published collations, superseded by the earlier 1518 use).

witnesses.name: Minuscule 330
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 330': described by Bernard de Montfaucon in his 1715 catalogue 'Bibliotheca Coisliniana olim Segueriana' (p. 249) of the Coislin collection it was then part of; later added to the list of NT manuscripts by Johann Scholz, and examined/collated by Paulin Martin and Eduard de Muralt. Corrected from 1864 (de Muralt's later catalogue, superseded by Montfaucon's earlier description).
witnesses.found: National Library of Russia, St Petersburg

witnesses.name: Minuscule 383
witnesses.year_known_basis: Examined and cited by J.J. Wettstein in his 1751-52 Novum Testamentum Graecum; later seen by Gaisford, Scholz, Pott and (in 1883) C.R. Gregory. Scholz added it to the standard list of NT manuscripts.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 424
witnesses.contents: Acts, Pauline epistles, Catholic epistles, Revelation
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 424' bibliography cites Andreas Christian Hwiid's 1785 monograph on the manuscript, titled with its Vienna imperial-library catalogue number 'Lambecii XXXIV' -- i.e. Peter Lambeck's catalogue (indexed by Nessel, 1690), consistent with this dataset's existing claim. Also examined by Treschow, Franz Karl Alter (whose 1786-87 Greek NT edition used it), Andreas Birch, and J.J. Griesbach; seen by Gregory in 1887.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 614
witnesses.year_known_basis: Important 'Western'-type witness in Acts (Aland Category III); drawn into critical use through F.H.A. Scrivener's and later J.H. Ropes's collations of Acts manuscripts.
witnesses.verify_note: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 614' says 'The manuscript was added to the list of New Testament manuscripts by Johann Martin Augustin Scholz' (no year given) and that 'C.R. Gregory saw the manuscript in 1886' -- it credits Scholz, not Scrivener/Ropes as this dataset's prior year_known_basis assumed, and gives no year for that listing, so 1860 is not confirmed (and the Scrivener/Ropes attribution appears to be wrong). Check the INTF Liste: https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste?docID=30614

witnesses.name: Minuscule 700
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 700': 'The codex was bought on the 28th April, 1882 for the British Museum, through the auspices of Edward Maunde Thompson.' Examined by Dean Burgon and collated by W.H. Simcox, Scrivener, and Hoskier. Corrected from 1875 (an unsupported estimate).

witnesses.name: Minuscule 892
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 892': 'The codex was acquired by the British Museum in 1887 from H. L. Dupuis.' Studied by Dean Burgon, later by J. Rendel Harris. Corrected from 1890 (an approximate estimate from the Additional-manuscript number range).

witnesses.name: Minuscule 1241
witnesses.year_known_basis: Catalogued at St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, in Vasilios Gardthausen's 1886 'Catalogus codicum Graecorum Sinaiticorum'.
witnesses.found: St Catherine's Monastery, Mount Sinai, Egypt

witnesses.name: Minuscule 1424
witnesses.contents: Complete NT with one small gap (Matthew 1:23-2:16)
witnesses.year_known_basis: One of many manuscripts removed in 1917 from the Kosinitza Monastery near Drama, Greece, in the upheavals of the Balkan Wars/WWI era; purchased in 1920 by Levi Franklin Gruber and entered the Gruber Collection at the Lutheran School of Theology at Chicago, the first complete Greek NT in minuscule script to enter modern Western study.
witnesses.found: Lutheran School of Theology at Chicago (Gruber Collection)
witnesses.note: Conventionally dated 9th or 10th century; archaizing script imitates majuscule models, so its precise date is debated.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 1582
witnesses.year_known_basis: Colophon-dated to 948, copied by the monk Ephraim (who also copied minuscule 1739 in the 10th c.). Identified as the leading witness of family 1 (f1) following Kirsopp Lake's 1902 study of the family (Texts and Studies VII.3, 'Codex 1 of the Gospels and Its Allies').
witnesses.verify_note: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 1582' says variants were cited in Hermann von Soden's apparatus (undated in this article) and that 'Burnett Hillman Streeter drew attention to the manuscript and its relationship with Family 1 ... in his [1924] book The Four Gospels: A Study of Origins' -- crediting Streeter (1924), not Kirsopp Lake's 1902 study of minuscule 1 (a different manuscript) as this dataset's prior year_known_basis assumed. The article otherwise says only that the manuscript 'came to scholarly notice in the early 20th century' without a precise year. Check the INTF Liste: https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste?docID=31582

witnesses.name: Minuscule 2053
witnesses.contents: Revelation, with the commentary of Oecumenius
witnesses.year_known_basis: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 2053' bibliography: Herman C. Hoskier, 'Der Apokalypse Text in dem Kommentar-Codex Messina 99,' American Journal of Philology 35 (1914) -- a study specifically of this manuscript, earlier than this dataset's prior assumption of Hoskier's 1929 'Concerning the Text of the Apocalypse'.

witnesses.name: Minuscule 2344
witnesses.contents: Acts, Catholic epistles, Pauline epistles, Revelation
witnesses.year_known_basis: Held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France; likely first catalogued in Henri Omont's 1888 'Inventaire sommaire des manuscrits grecs' of the BnF collection.
witnesses.verify_note: Wikipedia 'Minuscule 2344' has almost no discovery/cataloguing history: it says only that 'the text was collated by J. Schmid' (bibliography: 'Unbeachtete [overlooked] Apokalypse-Handschriften,' 1939) with 'a new collation ... by M. Davies' (1968) -- no mention of Henri Omont or an 1888 Bibliothèque nationale catalogue, so this dataset's 1888 claim is neither confirmed nor refuted (Schmid's 1939 title suggests the manuscript's significance for NT criticism, as opposed to its mere physical cataloguing, may actually date to 1939). Check the INTF Liste: https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/liste?docID=32344

count_over_time._note: Approximate running totals of catalogued Greek NT manuscripts known to scholarship. Early points are rough; label the chart 'approximate'. Confirm/refine using Gregory (1908), Aland (1963/1994), Wallace (2013), INTF current.

points.label: Gregory's list
points.note: Confirmed reasonable: Gregory's 1908 'Die griechischen Handschriften des Neuen Testaments' enumerated 2292 minuscules + 161 uncials + 1540 lectionaries (plus a handful of papyri known by then) = approx. 4000 total. No change made.

autographs.label: New Testament written
autographs.note: Conventional composition window for the NT books (Paul's letters from c. 50; John c. 90-100). 'Gap to the autographs' = midpoint of the earliest known witness minus 100 AD, matching data/comparison.json (P52 vs John, about 50 years).
